data: © Soviet Academy of Sciences (historical) — declassified materials. Position: Oceanus Procellarum, NASA's Lunar and Planetary Institute catalogue.

The first spacecraft to achieve a soft landing on the Moon and transmit photographs from the surface. Nine panoramic images ended the debate about whether landers would sink into deep lunar dust. A defining moment — the Moon could be reached.
First soft landing — required before any subsequent lunar surface operation, and the prerequisite proof-of-concept for every Mars lander since.

Luna 9 touched down in Oceanus Procellarum on February 3, 1966 — the first soft landing on another world. The 99 kg spherical capsule survived a 22 km/h impact by deploying inflatable cushions, then unfolded petals to right itself and transmitted the first photographs from the lunar surface. Operated for 3 days before battery exhaustion.
Luna 9 capsule mockup — 99 kg, spherical, with airbag-protected camera and four petal antennas.
Cutaway diagram of the Luna 9 hardware — Soviet engineers solved the soft-landing problem before NASA did.
Molniya-M rocket prepared at Baikonur — Luna 9 launched in a coast-coast Soviet/American race to the first soft landing.
First images of the lunar surface — coarse, low-bit-rate panoramas showing rocky regolith. The Manchester Jodrell Bank radio telescope intercepted the broadcast and published before the Soviets did.
Luna 9 panorama mosaic — first proof the lunar surface was solid enough to support a lander, ending years of speculation about deep dust drifts.
